system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 13 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2122-09-23 15:07:00 to 2122-10-06 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted with nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and epigastric pain, two days after a prior discharge for similar symptoms. He has a history of alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis, status post RFA and TACE for liver lesions, and is awaiting transplant. Workup revealed moderate fecal loading on CT, but no acute abdominal process. An upper endoscopy showed a friable 2 cm duodenal polyp with an ulcer, consistent with chronic duodenitis, but no bleeding; biopsy was deferred due to bleeding risk. A gastric emptying study demonstrated moderately delayed emptying, explaining persistent nausea. Iron supplements were discontinued as a potential contributor to symptoms. Metabolic alkalosis from vomiting resolved with supportive care. Diuretics were held initially for hypovolemia and restarted at discharge with reduced spironolactone. He improved on a gentle diet, tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home with medication adjustments and follow-up plans.
problems: Duodenal ulcer, unspecified as acute or chronic, without hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
Benign neoplasm of duodenum, jejunum, and ileum
Malignant neoplasm of liver, not specified as primary or secondary
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Other and unspecified alcohol dependence, in remission

Brief Hospital Course:
___ h/o HCV, HCC, alcohol cirrhosis s/p TACE who presented from 
home for deceased donor liver transplant ___. 

The liver transplant intraoperative course was complicated by 7L 
blood loss from IVC anastamosis. Intraoperatively pt received 4 
L of crystalloid, 11 units of red cells, 9 units of FFP, 3 units 
of platelets. Admitted to ICU intubated, no pressors. POD0 
overnight pt received 3 PRBCs, ___ FFP, 1 plts, 2 cryo with hct 
stable at ___. On POD1 urine output dropped off. His abdomen 
was tense, bladder pressures ___. He was taken back to OR for 
for washout and repair of bleeding vessel off IVC. He was given 
ad addtional 9 pRBCs, 3 plts, FFP 2, cryo 1. On POD2, he was 
taken back to OR for washout and oversewing of diaphragm for a 
diaphragmatic arterial hemorrhage. On POD3, pt was weaned to 
CPAP, and on POD4 he was extubated. 

On POD5, pt was transferred to the floor, out of bed to chair, 
and started on a regular diet. His weight was up to 113kg from 
admission weight of 100kg, so diuresis was started with lasix 
IV. Pt responded with good UOP and his renal function remained 
stable. His liver function tests continued to downtrend 
throughout the admission. Pain was controlled with dilaudid PO. 

For immunosuppression, he was started on mycofenolate on POD0 
and tacrolimus on POD1. His tacro level was followed daily and 
adjustments were made to his dose as necessary. He was given 
solumedrol on POD0-POD4, and then he was transitioned to 
prednisone, 35mg and then 20mg daily. He was started on bactrim, 
valcyte, fluconazole for prophylaxis. 

___ diabetes team was consulted for blood sugars in the 300s, 
and pt was started on insulin NPH standing and humalog sliding 
scale, which he will continue upon discharge given his 
steroid-induced hyperglycemia. 

It was reported that the liver donor had positive blood cultures 
of coag-negative staph, so surveillance blood cultures were sent 
which are no growth to date.

Pt worked with physical therapy and was able to walk using 
rolling walker, but it was recommended he go to rehab for 
physical therapy. 

His medial drain was taken out on POD9, and lateral drain taken 
out on POD13. Pt was discharged to rehab on POD13.

Discharge Instructions:
Please call the transplant clinic at ___ for fever > 
101, chills, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, inability 
to tolerate food, fluids or medications, yellowing of skin or 
eyes, increased abdominal pain, incisional redness, drainage or 
bleeding, dizziness or weakness, decreased urine output or dark, 
cloudy urine, swelling of abdomen or ankles, or any other 
concerning symptoms.

You will have labwork drawn every ___ and ___ with 
results to the transplant clinic. (Fax ___ CBC, Chem 
10, AST, ALT, Alk Phos, T Bili, Trough prograf level. On the 
days you have your labs drawn, do not take your prograf until 
your labs are drawn. Bring your prograf with you so you may take 
your medication as soon as your labwork has been drawn.

Please follow your medication card, keep it updated with any 
dosage changes, and always bring your card with you to any 
clinic or hospital visits.
You may shower. Allow the water to run over your incision and 
pat area dry. No rubbing, no lotions or powder near the 
incision. You may leave the incision open to the air. The 
staples are removed approximately 3 weeks following your 
transplant.
No tub baths or swimming
No driving if taking narcotic pain medications

Avoid direct sun exposure. Wear protective clothing and a hat, 
and always wear sunscreen when you go outdoors.

Drink enough fluids to keep your urine light in color. Your 
appetite will return with time. Eat small frequent meals, and 
you may supplement with things like carnation instant breakfast 
or Ensure.

Check your blood sugars and blood pressure at home. Report 
consistently elevated values to the transplant clinic

Do not increase, decrease, stop or start medications without 
consultation with the transplant clinic at ___. There 
are significant drug interactions with anti-rejection 
medications which must be considered in medication management 
following transplant

DATE:  ___.

TYPE OF EXAMINATION:  Chest AP portable single view.

FINDINGS:  AP single view of the chest has been obtained with patient in

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel, one of your transplant surgeons. You're here today for your liver transplant, and we’re going to take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ve been waiting for this. I just hope everything goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history carefully. You’ve had a tough road with hepatitis C, cirrhosis, and the liver cancer treated with TACE. But you’re in good hands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling weak, and my belly’s been swollen. Is that all going to get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the transplant should resolve the cirrhosis and portal hypertension. The ascites should improve, and your energy will come back over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’m a little nervous about the surgery itself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. The surgery is complex, but we do it regularly. You’ll be under general anesthesia, and we’ll monitor you closely in the ICU after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach issues—duodenitis and all that—will that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your duodenitis. It’s not a barrier to transplant. We’ll manage it with pantoprazole and monitor for any bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I trust you. Let’s do this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you made it through the transplant surgery. It was a long operation, and there was significant blood loss—about 7 liters—due to a bleed at the IVC connection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no… is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was serious, but we managed it. You received multiple blood products during surgery and stayed in the ICU overnight. You’re stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much. Was I awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, you were intubated and on a ventilator. We’re watching your breathing closely. The chest X-ray shows a new right pleural effusion, but it’s not large.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it should resolve as you heal. We’ll keep monitoring it. Your liver ultrasound shows good blood flow, which is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, you had another bleed overnight. We took you back to surgery to control it. You lost more blood, but we’ve stabilized you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another surgery? I didn’t expect that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon after major transplants. We found a vessel near the IVC. You’re doing well now, and we’ll keep a close eye on your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You had another procedure last night. There was a small bleed from a diaphragmatic artery, so we went back to fix it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three surgeries in two days… am I going to be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re stable now. No more bleeding. Your labs are improving. The repeat ultrasound shows the hematoma around the liver is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hematoma? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small collection of blood from the surgery. It’s not expanding, and your body will reabsorb it over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re weaning the ventilator. You should be off it tomorrow. Your kidney function is stable, and your liver enzymes are starting to drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’re off the ventilator and on CPAP. Your breathing is strong. The chest X-ray shows the pleural effusion is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe easier already. When can I eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on clear liquids today. If you tolerate it, we’ll advance to a regular diet tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. I’ve missed real food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll take it slow. Your gut has been through a lot. We’re also starting immunosuppressants—tacrolimus and mycophenolate—to protect your new liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember those from the list. Any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your levels closely. Tacrolimus can affect kidneys and raise blood sugar, but we’ll adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The chest X-ray shows better lung expansion. We removed the Swan-Ganz catheter. You’re off CPAP now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I sit up more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and physical therapy will help you get stronger. You’ll move to the floor tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Welcome to the floor. You’re out of bed and walking a bit. Your weight is up—113 kg from 100—so we’re starting IV furosemide to help with fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel bloated. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, after major surgery and blood transfusions, fluid retention is common. The diuretic will help, and your kidneys are doing fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver function is improving—AST and ALT are down to 37 and 86. Bilirubin is nearly normal. The biopsy of your new liver shows mild preservation injury, no rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very good. It means your liver is adapting well. We’re also watching your blood sugar—steroids can raise it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mine’s been high. Do I have diabetes now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s steroid-induced hyperglycemia. We’ve started insulin, and you’ll likely need it for a while, but it may improve as we taper the steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The donor had a blood culture positive for coagulase-negative staph, so we’re being cautious. Your blood cultures are negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could I get that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible but unlikely. We’re giving you fluconazole, Bactrim, and valganciclovir to prevent infections. You’re on heparin to prevent clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your cultures are negative. No sign of infection. Your tacrolimus level is 9.2—perfect. We’ll keep it there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been walking with the walker. PT says I need rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve made great progress, but you’ll benefit from inpatient rehab to regain strength and independence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture is negative. No UTI. The abdominal drain is draining less, so we’ll consider removing it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We removed the medial drain yesterday. The lateral one will come out in a couple of days. You’re healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to get out of here. What do I need to watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the clinic if you have fever, nausea, vomiting, yellow skin, or pain. Check your blood sugar and blood pressure daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take them exactly as prescribed. Don’t stop or change anything without calling us. The anti-rejection drugs have many interactions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final plan: You’ll go to rehab tomorrow. The lateral drain comes out this morning. Your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I couldn’t have made it through this without your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did the hard part—your body is healing. Keep up the good work, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged to rehab. Continue your meds, monitor your symptoms, and follow up with the transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be alive and on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but your new liver is working well. Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay strong, and we’ll keep supporting you every step of the way.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted for a deceased donor liver transplant due to alcoholic and hepatitis C-related cirrhosis with hepatocellular carcinoma. The transplant surgery was complicated by significant intraoperative bleeding requiring multiple transfusions and two re-explorations for hemorrhage control. He remained intubated in the ICU for several days, with gradual improvement in respiratory and renal function. His liver enzymes normalized over time, and a biopsy of the allograft showed only mild preservation injury without rejection. He developed steroid-induced hyperglycemia, managed with insulin, and was monitored for potential infection due to the donor's coagulase-negative staph. He progressed well with physical therapy, had abdominal drains removed, and was discharged to inpatient rehabilitation on postoperative day 13 with a stable condition and a full regimen of immunosuppressive and prophylactic medications.
